citations.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

derivations.claim: If $k=1$, every feasible $Q$ is a unit column $q$, so $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=q^TAq=R_A(q)$. By [F2], its minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, which is $\lambda_1$ in the increasing order of the Statement.

Suppose $k\ge2$. By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$, and let $U$ be the matrix with these columns. For any feasible $Q$, put $C=U^TQ$; then $C^TC=I_k$ and $Q^TAQ=C^T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)C$. Writing $c_{ij}$ for the entries of $C$ and $p_i=\sum_{j=1}^k c_{ij}^2$, direct expansion of the diagonal sum gives $\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i p_i$.

The matrix $P=CC^T$ is symmetric and idempotent because $C^TC=I_k$. Hence it is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of $C$, and $p_i=e_i^TPe_i=\|Pe_i\|_2^2$ lies in $[0,1]$. Also $\sum_i p_i=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}^2=\sum_j(C^TC)_{jj}=k$.

Using $\sum_i p_i=k$, subtract the bottom-$k$ eigenvalue sum to obtain $$\sum_i\lambda_i p_i-\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=\sum_{i=1}^k(\lambda_k-\lambda_i)(1-p_i)+\sum_{i=k+1}^n(\lambda_i-\lambda_k)p_i\ge0.$$ Every term on the right is nonnegative. Taking $Q=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)$ gives equality, so the stated minimum is attained. This proves the claim for $k\ge2$ as well as the $k=1$ case of step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The statement requires n≥1 and 1≤k≤n; an empty matrix is outside the domain.

Step 1.1 proves the k=1 Rayleigh boundary.
Step 3.1 remains nonnegative when λ_k is repeated; the stated eigenbasis attains the minimum.
Steps 1.1 and 3.1 cover k=1 and k=n; the latter has an empty upper-index sum.

The statement is a minimum formula, not an if-and-only-if claim.

citations.quote:
Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: Write $x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i e_i$. The unique decompositions of two vectors add, and scalar multiples of a decomposition remain decompositions, so uniqueness makes $P_E$ linear. If $x\in E$, its decomposition is $x+0$, hence $P_Ex=x$. Therefore $x=P_Ex=\sum_i x_iP_Ee_i$, and the projected coordinate vectors span $E$.

Start with $q_0$ if supplied, then process $v_i=P_Ee_i$ in order. Each residual $r_i=v_i-\sum_j\langle v_i,b_j\rangle b_j$ lies in $E$ and is orthogonal to every previously accepted orthonormal vector $b_j$. If $r_i=0$, then $v_i$ is already in their span; if $r_i\ne0$, appending $r_i/\|r_i\|_2$ preserves orthonormality and the span of all processed vectors. By induction, after the finite scan the accepted list is orthonormal and spans the initial vector together with all $P_Ee_i$. Step 1.1 shows this span is $E$, and the initial unit vector is first when present.

boundaries.evidence: If E={0} and no q0 is supplied, steps 1.1–2.1 show all projected residuals are zero and the empty list spans E.
Step 2.1 explicitly discards each zero residual without changing the accumulated span.
For a one-dimensional E, step 2.1 appends the first nonzero projected coordinate vector and skips the remaining dependent vectors.
Steps 1.1–2.1 prove the construction for arbitrary finite dimension, including repeated-eigenvalue eigenspaces.
Step 2.1 handles the finite scan when m=1, whose sole coordinate vector spans any one-dimensional E.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $w_{ij}=w_{ji}\ge0$ and $w_{ii}=0$. Define $d_i=\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has vertex set $V$ and edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; isolated vertices are singleton connected components. Put $V_+=\{i\in V:d_i>0\}$, let $D_+$ and $L_+$ be the principal submatrices indexed by $V_+$, and, only when $V_+\ne\varnothing$, define $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}=D_+^{-1/2}L_+D_+^{-1/2}$ on $\mathbb R^{V_+}$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $f^TLf=\sum_i d_i f_i^2-\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}f_if_j$. Replacing $d_i$ by $\sum_jw_{ij}$, using $w_{ij}=w_{ji}$ to identify the two square sums, and collecting terms gives $f^TLf=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(f_i^2-2f_if_j+f_j^2)=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$.
The displayed sum is nonnegative for every $f$, and $L$ is symmetric because both $D$ and $W$ are symmetric. Therefore $L$ is positive semidefinite.

If $Lf=0$, then $f^TLf=0$. By step 1.1 this is a finite sum of nonnegative terms, so every term with $w_{ij}>0$ vanishes and $f_i=f_j$ on every support edge. Equality propagates along each finite path, hence $f$ is constant on every connected component, including an isolated singleton.

Conversely, suppose $f$ is constant on each support component. For each vertex $i$, every $j$ with $w_{ij}>0$ lies in the same component, so $f_i=f_j$. Hence $(Lf)_i=d_if_i-\sum_jw_{ij}f_j=\sum_jw_{ij}(f_i-f_j)=0$ for every $i$, and $Lf=0$. The two inclusions give the stated kernel equality.

boundaries.reason: The statement assumes n≥1; the empty vertex set is outside its domain.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 gives zero energy when every weight is zero; steps 2.2 and 3.1 then identify the kernel as all vectors, constant on singleton components.
For n=1 the sums are empty and the sole vertex is an isolated singleton; steps 1.1–3.1 apply.
Steps 2.2 and 3.1 cover disconnected support graphs and isolated components.

boundaries.reason: There is no endpoint parameter in this identity or kernel characterization.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $w_{ij}=w_{ji}\ge0$ and $w_{ii}=0$. Define $d_i=\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, and $L=D-W$. The support graph has vertex set $V$ and edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$; isolated vertices are singleton connected components. Let $n\ge1$, $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and zero-diagonal. Define $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$, $L=D-W$, and $V_+=\{i:d_i>0\}$. For $A\subseteq V$, put $A^c=V\setminus A$, $\operatorname{cut}(A,A^c)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in A^c}w_{ij}$, and $\operatorname{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_i$. For a partition $\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $V$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, define $$\operatorname{RatioCut}(\mathcal A)=\sum_{r=1}^k\frac{\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)}{|A_r|}.$$ For a partition of $V_+$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, each of positive volume, define $$\operatorname{Ncut}(\mathcal A)=\sum_{r=1}^k\frac{\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)}{\operatorname{vol}(A_r)}.$$ For these partitions, the RatioCut indicator column is $h_r=\mathbf1_{A_r}/\sqrt{|A_r|}$, and the Ncut indicator column is $h_r=\mathbf1_{A_r}/\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(A_r)}$, extended by zero on isolated vertices.

Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$, let $W$ be symmetric, nonnegative, and zero-diagonal, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sum_jw_{ij})$, let $L=D-W$, and let the support graph have edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$. For every $f\in\mathbb R^n$, $$f^TLf=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2.$$ Consequently $L$ is positive semidefinite and $$\ker L=\{f\in\mathbb R^n:f\text{ is constant on each connected component of the support graph}\},$$ including isolated singleton components.

derivations.claim: The supports of distinct RatioCut indicator columns are disjoint, and each column has $|A_r|$ entries equal to $|A_r|^{-1/2}$. Thus each column has squared norm $1$ and distinct columns have inner product $0$, so $H_R^TH_R=I_k$.
The supports of distinct Ncut indicator columns are disjoint, and $h_r^TDh_r=\operatorname{vol}(A_r)^{-1}\sum_{i\in A_r}d_i=1$. Distinct columns have $D$-inner product $0$, so $H_N^TDH_N=I_k$.

By [F3], the energy of a RatioCut indicator column is $\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}(h_i-h_j)^2$. Terms with both indices inside or both outside $A_r$ vanish. Each ordered crossing pair has squared difference $|A_r|^{-1}$; symmetry makes the two directed crossing sums equal, so the factor $1/2$ leaves $h_r^TLh_r=\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)/|A_r|$.

For a Ncut indicator column the same finite energy sum has zero terms except across $A_r$ and its complement, and each crossing squared difference is $\operatorname{vol}(A_r)^{-1}$. Pairing the two equal directed sums gives $h_r^TLh_r=\operatorname{cut}(A_r,A_r^c)/\operatorname{vol}(A_r)$.

By the stated trace definition, $\operatorname{tr}(H_R^TLH_R)=\sum_r h_r^TLh_r$ and $\operatorname{tr}(H_N^TLH_N)=\sum_r h_r^TLh_r$. Summing steps 1.3 and 1.4 gives the RatioCut and Ncut identities, while steps 1.1 and 1.2 give their respective indicator constraints.

Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$, let $W$ be symmetric, nonnegative, and zero-diagonal, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sum_jw_{ij})$, let $L=D-W$, and let the support graph have edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $w_{ij}>0$. Let $W,D,L,V,V_+$ be as in the finite weighted graph definition. For a square matrix $B$, set $\operatorname{tr}(B)=\sum_i B_{ii}$. If $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ partition $V$, define $H_R\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ by $(H_R)_{ir}=|A_r|^{-1/2}$ for $i\in A_r$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $H_R^TH_R=I_k$ and $\operatorname{RatioCut}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\operatorname{tr}(H_R^TLH_R)$. If $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ partition $V_+$, define $H_N\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ by $(H_N)_{ir}=\operatorname{vol}(A_r)^{-1/2}$ for $i\in A_r$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $H_N^TDH_N=I_k$ and $\operatorname{Ncut}(A_1,\ldots,A_k)=\operatorname{tr}(H_N^TLH_N)$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$ be its real eigenvalues repeated with multiplicity, and define $\operatorname{tr}(B)=\sum_i B_{ii}$ for square $B$. For $1\le k\le n$, $$\min_{Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ Q^TQ=I_k}\operatorname{tr}(Q^TAQ)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i.$$ The minimum is attained by taking the columns of $Q$ to be orthonormal eigenvectors for the $k$ smallest eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; when an eigenvalue at the cutoff is repeated, the minimizer need not be unique.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F3], $L$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. If $x\in\mathbb R^{|V_+|}$, extend it by zero on isolates to $\widetilde x\in\mathbb R^n$; then $x^TL_+x=\widetilde x^TL\widetilde x\ge0$, so $L_+$ is positive semidefinite. Since $D_+^{-1/2}$ is a real diagonal matrix, $y^TL_{\mathrm{sym},+}y=(D_+^{-1/2}y)^TL_+(D_+^{-1/2}y)\ge0$. Thus both Laplacians in the Statement are positive semidefinite.

For every partition of $V$ into $k$ nonempty sets, [F4] supplies a feasible $H_R$ for the real constraint $H^TH=I_k$ with trace equal to that partition's RatioCut. The relaxed feasible set therefore contains every discrete indicator matrix, so the infimum over the relaxed feasible set is at most the minimum over the finite nonempty family of partitions.

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ partition $V_+$. By [F4], their normalized indicators, restricted to $V_+$, satisfy $H^TD_+H=I_k$ and have trace objective equal to Ncut. Indeed, if $i$ is isolated then $d_i=0$ and $\sum_jw_{ij}=0$ with $w_{ij}\ge0$ forces every $w_{ij}=0$, so row and column $i$ of $L$ vanish; extending $H$ by zero on isolates leaves the active trace unchanged. Thus the active real feasible set contains every discrete Ncut indicator, and the infimum over the active real feasible set is at most $N_k$.

The matrix $L$ is real symmetric by [F1]. Applying [F5] with $A=L$ gives $\min_{H^TH=I_k}\operatorname{tr}(H^TLH)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(L)$, attained by orthonormal eigenvectors for the $k$ smallest eigenvalues. Together with step 1.2 this is the claimed RatioCut lower bound.

The diagonal entries of $D_+$ are strictly positive, so $Q=D_+^{1/2}H$ is a bijection from $H^TD_+H=I_k$ to $Q^TQ=I_k$. It also gives $\operatorname{tr}(H^TL_+H)=\operatorname{tr}(Q^TD_+^{-1/2}L_+D_+^{-1/2}Q)=\operatorname{tr}(Q^TL_{\mathrm{sym},+}Q)$. Applying [F5] to $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}$ gives the stated Ncut relaxed minimum and optimizer $H=D_+^{-1/2}Q$; with step 1.3 this is the claimed lower bound.

If $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}q=\lambda q$ and $u=D_+^{-1/2}q$, multiplying by $D_+^{1/2}$ gives $L_+u=\lambda D_+u$. Conversely, if $L_+u=\lambda D_+u$, then $q=D_+^{1/2}u$ satisfies $L_{\mathrm{sym},+}q=\lambda q$. Thus the symmetric normalized problem is equivalent to the generalized eigenproblem stated.

Every Ncut part is a nonempty subset of $V_+$, so its volume is positive; an isolate has zero volume but is excluded from $N_k$ and can only be reinserted as a separately reported singleton. Steps 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, and 2.2 compare feasible sets and compute the lower bounds; they do not bound the RatioCut or Ncut value after an arbitrary rounding.

The union rule keeps an edge selected in either direction, so its undirected edges are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$. The mutual rule keeps only edges selected in both directions, so its only edge is $\{1,2\}$. Both weight matrices satisfy [F1].

In the union graph, the only crossing edge for $A_1=\{1,2\}$ and $A_2=\{3\}$ is $\{2,3\}$, of weight $1$; hence both one-sided cuts equal $1$. In the mutual graph there is no crossing edge, so both cuts equal $0$.
By [F2], the union RatioCut is $1/2+1=3/2$, while the mutual RatioCut is $0/2+0/1=0$. Thus the fixed data, neighbor count, and partition have different cut values under the two symmetrizations.

**Inputs.** Integers $n,p\ge1$, data $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, a fixed deterministic graph-construction procedure $G:(\mathbb R^p)^n\to\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, mode $\texttt{ratio}$ or $\texttt{normalized}$, and cluster count $k\ge1$. In normalized mode also supply a Boolean row-normalization option, defaulting to false.

1. Compute $W=G(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. Reject the input unless $W$ is symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, and zero-diagonal. Set $d_i=\sum_jw_{ij}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)$, $L=D-W$, and $V_+=\{i:d_i>0\}$.

2. In ratio mode require $k\le n$, use all vertices in increasing index order, and set $M=L$. In normalized mode, if $V_+=\varnothing$, return every vertex as a separately reported singleton with status $\texttt{no-positive-degree-vertices}$.
